chronicles-story-3.content:
For almost a hundred years, Khar-Durim tried to regain its freedom.

@@LORE_IMAGE:chronicles-story-3@@

Miners killed their supervisors and barricaded themselves in the shafts.

Old warriors stole weapons from elven warehouses.

In Gor-Dum, patrols that ventured too deep underground disappeared.

Mechanisms in Brumwald were breaking down, and there was no indication of failure the day before.

In Kar-Dor, caches full of swords dating back to the times before the occupation were found.

Revolts broke out.

And they went out.

Each time, someone believed that this time it would be different.

Each time, Vaelthar responded with soldiers.

After a few days or weeks, reprisals came.

New outposts.

New executions.

New bans.

And then Khar-Durim went back to work.

After a hundred years, the hardest part was not finding a dwarf willing to die for freedom.

There was never a shortage of these.

The hardest thing was to find a dwarf who still believed that his death would change anything.

Thorgrim

Thorgrim of the Ironhammers was born into a world where Elvish banners already hung over Dur-Gari. He did not remember the day Khar-Durim was conquered.

But he remembered people who remembered him.

As a child, he heard stories of a time when a dwarven warrior did not need an elf's permission to carry an axe.

About ships leaving the port with goods belonging to the dwarves.

Of the First Forge, whose fire would burn even before some of the present cities existed.

For the elders, these were memories.

For Thorgrim - stories.

By the time he grew up, many of the people who told them were dead.

The Iron Hammers taught him two things.

How to work.

And how to hate.

So he worked in the same mines from which the wealth later flowed to Sah'Rava.

He saw dwarves guarding other dwarves.

He saw elven overseers counting the output.

He saw the old tunnels being deepened every year by the same people Vaelthar had supposedly conquered to keep them from digging.

Thorgrim didn't need the chronicles to understand the elven king's hypocrisy.

He just needed to look at his own hands.

Over time, his name began to appear more and more often.

First in one mine.

Then in several.

Later outside the lands of the Iron Hammers.

Not because Thorgrim made great speeches. He was doing something much rarer.

He listened.

He listened to stories about subsequent rebellions.

He asked where they started.

Who knew about them before.

Who didn't know.

How long did it take the elves to gather their soldiers?

Which clan came to help.

Who didn't make it.

Who didn't even know he should.

Years later, he came to a conclusion that sounded almost offensive in its simplicity.

Dwarves have never lacked courage.

They missed each other.

Thorgrim had no plans for another rebellion.

Not yet.

First he started traveling.

Officially as a miner.

Sometimes a dealer.

Sometimes a man was sent to another mine.

The Elven empire was powerful, but after a hundred years of occupation, it also had its weaknesses.

Routine.

The overseer, whose grandfather was guarding the same shaft, did not expect that the war would start tomorrow.

The guard at the gate knew the faces of the workers passing by.

Reports from Khar-Durim have been saying more or less the same thing for decades. Extraction.

Transport.

Petty sabotage.

Arrests.

Composure.

Vaelthar no longer saw the dwarves as defeated enemies.

He began to see subjects.

Thorgrim intended to take advantage of this mistake.

But first he had to convince the four clans that they were still something more.

Four answers

The easiest was with the Iron Hammers.

Not because they were the most obedient to Thorgrim.

Because they were the angriest.

It was enough to say "uprising" for ten men to reach for their axes.

Thorgrim had to teach them something more difficult.

Waiting.

"If we strike today, how many will follow us?" - he asked.

- Sufficiently.

-It's not a number.

-More than last time.

—We lost last time.

Not everyone liked these answers.

But Thorgrim didn't need another heroic death.

Khar-Durim had enough of them already.

He needed a victory. It was different with the Stone Shields.

Borgrim remembered the first war.

He remembered Khar-Durim from before the captivity.

He also remembered how confident his leaders had been back then.

Kar-Dor had walls.

Deep Forge mountains.

Iron Hammers of Warriors.

Copper Gears of the Machine.

Everyone was convinced that he would survive.

Borgrim saw where this certainty ended.

When Thorgrim first told him about the joint uprising, the old dwarf remained silent for a long time.

—Four clans have already fought against Vaelthar.

- NO.

Borgrim looked at him.

Thorgrim repeated:

- They didn't fight. Everyone defended their own door. Vaelthar just moved from one to the next.

-And now?

- Now if he knocks on one door, all four will open it.

Borgrim apparently smiled then for the first time.

Some say that it was on this day that the Stone Shields decided to support Thorgrim.

Borgrim later denied this.

However, he never said on what day he actually did it.

Haldrek of the Copper Gears was waiting in Brumwald. Haldrek needed no convincing that elven rule should end.

He needed to be convinced that Thorgrim was not just another man planning to die more spectacularly than his predecessors.

Apparently he started the first conversation with a question:

- How many weapons do you have?

Thorgrim gave a number.

- Too little. How many people?

Thorgrim replied.

- Too little. Food?

Another answer.

Haldrek shook his head.

— Definitely not enough.

— That's why I'm here.

Haldrek looked at him.

- That's good. For a moment I was afraid that you had come to ask for my blessing.

It was Haldrek who began to turn the idea into something that could actually work.

The uprising needed more than just warriors.

It needed food.

Roads.

Warehouses.

Tools.

People who know which elven gates can be blocked and which can be opened.

Mechanisms that will stop working at the right moment.

Carts that will carry one more box for months than stated in the documents.

The Copper Gears began preparations. Slowly.

Quiet.

No heroism.

Just like building a machine that no one can see before it is turned on.

The Deep Forges were the hardest.

Varkun had no doubt that Khar-Durim should be free.

He doubted that Thorgrim was the man to free them.

In Gor-Dum the memory of Groudon was stronger than anywhere else.

The Deep Forges believed that the mountains belonged to the children of Earth.

They didn't need the man from the Ironhammers to remind them of that.

"Why should we follow you?" Varkun asked.

Thorgrim replied:

- You shouldn't.

Varkun frowned.

- NO?

- You should walk next to me.

There was no crown.

There was no king yet.

Thorgrim did not ask the four clans to become one.

He just asked them to do something together once.

Varkun did not respond immediately.

But Thorgrim left Gor-Dum with what he had come for.

A promise.

When the day comes, the Deep Forges will rise. One problem remains.

The biggest.

The dwarves had heard similar promises before.

Their fathers heard them too.

And grandparents.

Someone said that this time all the clans will stand together.

Someone else assured that elves were weak.

Someone else swore that one big blow would be enough.

Then came the executions.

Thorgrim could have had Borgrim.

He could have had Haldrek.

He could have had Varkun.

He might even have had a plan.

But the uprising cannot be won by four leaders.

He needed miners.

Blacksmiths.

Farmers.

Guardians.

Craftsmen.

Thousands of people who, after a hundred years, were about to risk the lives of their families because someone once again told them:

this time we will win.

And that's when a fire appeared in the mountains.

Entei

The first stories told of a huge Pokémon seen high in the north. Some claimed that its ridge resembled a smoking volcano.

Others, that the earth trembled under his paws.

Still others were sure they heard him roar from the other side of the mountain.

No sane person took these stories seriously.

Until Thorgrim saw him for himself.

There is no single agreed story about Thorgrim's first meeting with Entei.

The Iron Hammers claim that Thorgrim found him after many days of wandering and stood before him unarmed.

The Deep Forges maintain that Entei himself emerged from the fire hidden deep beneath Khar-Duri.

In Brumwald, however, you can hear that Thorgrim simply got lost during one of his journeys, and the rest of the story was added later to make it sound better.

Thorgrim never settled the dispute.

When asked years later why Entei decided to stay with him, he replied:

-Ask Entei.

Nobody tried.

All that is known is that Thorgrim did not capture him.

He didn't beat it.

He did not force obedience.

When he returned from the mountains, Entei was walking next to him.

And that was enough.

The news spread very quickly.

Work in the mines was stopped when he passed by on a nearby road.

The dwarves were leaving their homes. Some followed him for several kilometers just to see if the stories were true.

Were.

Entei did not speak.

He didn't promise victory.

He didn't say Groudon sent him to the dwarves.

He just walked next to Thorgrim.

After a hundred years of failure, this was exactly what Khar-Durim needed.

Not another promise.

Proof that something has changed.

If a being capable of walking away in any direction chose Thorgrim himself, perhaps it was worth at least listening to what the dwarf had to say.

If Entei believed that he was worth staying with...

maybe this time there really was a chance.

Not certainty.

Not a prophecy.

Chance.

After a hundred years, it was more than anyone remembered.

Not everyone liked the importance that began to be assigned to Entei.

Haldrek is said to have warned Thorgrim:

"A little more and they'll start saying Groudon sent it to you."

- They're already talking.

"And what are you going to do about it?"

- Nothing.

- It's dangerous.

Thorgrim looked at Entei lying by the fire. "If I make them believe that Groudon sent him, I will be a liar." If I forbid them to believe it, I will be a fool.

Haldrek sighed.

"You're starting to sound like a king."

- We have no king.

- I know. That's why it worries me.

One Khar-Durim

From then on, preparations accelerated.

There were no longer four plans.

There was one.

The Iron Hammers were intended to prepare people for battle.

Those whom the elves left in the auxiliary guards were to turn their weapons against their own commanders at the appropriate moment.

The miners knew where the warehouses were.

Blacksmiths knew how many weapons could be made before anyone noticed a difference in the use of metal.

The Stone Shields prepared passages, defense points, and places where a small group could stop a larger elven column.

Old tunnels were re-mapped.

The walls were not looked at in terms of how to defend them against attack from outside.

This time they asked how to recover them from the inside.

The Copper Gears counted everything.

Food.

Carts.

Weapon. Days.

Distances.

Haldrek knew that a victorious army must also eat.

So Brumwald gathered supplies slowly so that the elvish reports would still be accurate.

One bag here.

Two there.

Some grain recorded as spoiled.

Several crates sent to the wrong address.

Little lies.

For months.

Enough little lies can feed an army.

The Deep Forges prepared the warriors.

And roads the elves didn't know.

Under the northern mountains there were passages carved long before the occupation.

They didn't lead everywhere.

They were not secret tunnels capable of winning the war.

But they allowed people and messages to move where elven patrols thought impossible.

Varkun gathered his men in silence.

It was increasingly said in Gor-Dum that the First Fire had not yet been extinguished.

He's just waiting.

Help also began to come from beyond Khar-Durim.

Not under human banners.

Not with Valoria's soldiers.

King Aldrin IV had no intention of declaring war on Vaelthar. But ships sometimes lost some of their cargo.

Merchants sometimes received payment for goods that they never officially sold.

The weapons crossed the sea hidden under other cargo.

Information about the movements of Elven ships reached people who should not have known them.

Few people on Khar-Durim knew where exactly the help was coming from.

Thorgrim knew.

Haldrek too.

That was enough for now.

Months passed.

Every day there was a risk that someone would speak too soon.

That an elven patrol will find the warehouse.

That the dwarf being interrogated will crack.

That one mistake will destroy everything.

Thorgrim waited.

The Iron Hammers were impatient.

Varkun asked how much more.

Borgrim replied that it was as much as necessary.

Each time Haldrek found one more thing that was missing.

And Entei waited with them.

Finally Haldrek placed the final tally before Thorgrim.

Food.

Weapon.

People.

Dear. Outposts.

Changes of guard.

Ships.

Everything that could be counted.

Thorgrim looked at him.

-And?

Haldrek read his own numbers for a moment.

— If you're asking if we can win, I don't know.

- That's not what I'm asking.

Haldrek looked up.

— If you're asking if we'll ever be better prepared...

He submitted the document.

- NO.

That was enough.

The First Forge

All that remains is to determine the signal.

Not a message.

Not a messenger.

Not a date written on paper an elf might find.

Something every clan will understand.

Borgrim suggested bells.

Haldrek rejected the idea. The elves could have silenced them.

Varkun wanted fire on the mountain peaks.

Thorgrim had a different answer.

The First Forge. For almost a hundred years, its hearth had remained cold.

Vaelthar extinguished them after the conquest of Khar-Durim.

Not because he needed her metal.

The first Forge was not the largest.

It wasn't even particularly efficient.

She was a symbol.

According to dwarven tradition, its fire burned even before many clan seats were established.

That's why the elves ordered it to be put out.

And that was why Thorgrim wanted to reignite it.

The plan was simple.

When everything is ready, the message will reach the four clans.

Not with the date of creation.

With just one sentence:

“Look at the Forge.”

And later:

"When the First Forge burns again, Khar-Durim will rise."

Night came.

In Dur-Garim, elven patrols walked the same streets as always.

The mills were turning in Brumwald.

In Kar-Dor, the guards took turns on the walls.

There were forges in Gor-Dum.

Another shift was ending in the mines.

It was an ordinary evening for the elves.

After almost a hundred years, they all looked alike. Thorgrim stood before the First Forge.

Entei stood next to him.

The fireplace was cold.

It was covered with ash so old that no one present remembered the fire that had left it.

Thorgrim placed his hand on the stone.

For a moment nothing happened.

He didn't make a speech.

There was no crowd.

There was no coronation.

It wasn't even certain whether any of them would be alive in a few days.

Thorgrim looked at Entei.

The Pokémon walked over to the fire pit.

And after a hundred years, the First Forge caught fire.

The fire was small at first.

Then he climbed higher.

The light fell on the old walls.

On the stone.

For symbols that the elves could never completely remove.

The dwarf standing at the entrance stared for a moment, as if he had forgotten what he was supposed to do.

Thorgrim turned to him.

-Go.

The messenger ran.

The first news reached the men of the Iron Hammers. Then to the hidden points of the Stone Shields.

The riders moved towards Brumwald.

Others disappeared on the northern routes towards Gor-Dum.

In one of the underground passages, a tired messenger found a group of dwarves waiting.

One of them stood up.

- What happened?

The messenger tried to catch his breath.

Then he smiled.

- The forge is burning.

For a moment no one spoke.

The dwarf standing across from him reached for his axe.

- So here we go.

That night in the four parts of Khar-Durim the dwarves laid down their picks.

They opened hiding places.

They pulled out weapons wrapped in cloth and hidden for years.

The guards looked at the elven commanders they had saluted only hours earlier.

In Kar-Dor, relevant crossings were closed.

The mechanisms stopped in Brumwald.

Old tunnels were being opened in Gor-Dum.

No one has ever won a battle.

No elven banner was torn down.

Khar-Durim still belonged to Vaelthar.

But for the first time in almost a hundred years, the four clans did not wait for one of them to rebel.

They were all waiting for the same fire. And they all saw him.

Flames rose above the First Forge.

And with them, a hundred years of waiting ended.

Khar-Durim was established.

The dwarf standing opposite the messenger reached for his axe.

- So here we go.

On the same night, similar words were spoken in dozens of places.

In the mines.

In the forges.

In the Brumwald warehouses.

Beyond the walls of Kar-Dor.

In the underground corridors of Gor-Dum.

For almost a hundred years, every dwarven uprising began the same way.

Someone grabbed the gun first.

Someone killed the elven guard first.

Someone was the first to tear down Vaelthar's banner.

And then he waited for the rest of the Khar-Durim to follow him.

This time no one had to wait.

All of Khar-Durim took up arms at once.

Night of fire

In the Iron Hammer mines, work ended like every day.

An elven foreman walked among the workers, checking the output.

Pickaxes hit the rock.

Once.

Second.

Third. Then one of the miners stopped.

The elf looked at him.

— Go back to work.

The dwarf rested his pickaxe on the ground.

Another thump faded past him.

Then the next one.

After a while, the entire tunnel was silent.

— I said: get back to work.

Nobody moved.

The overseer reached for his gun.

And then the dwarven guard behind him did the same.

Only he pointed the blade in the other direction.

For a hundred years, Vaelthar used the dwarves to guard his own people.

He paid for that decision that night.

Guards opened weapons warehouses.

Workers pulled out hidden axes.

Blacksmiths handed out swords that, according to elvish records, were never made.

The posts were cut off from each other.

Messengers disappeared into the tunnels before they could deliver the message.

Where the elves tried to gather larger forces, they found that the gate that had worked perfectly yesterday suddenly refused to open.

Or that the bridge was raised.

Or that the road where reinforcements were supposed to come is blocked.

For months, the four clans had prepared for this night.

Now all the little lies, thefts, hidden chests and deliberately broken mechanisms began to matter. At Dur-Garim, Thorgrim did not attempt to take the city from outside.

He didn't have to.

The Iron Hammers were already there.

The dwarves worked in the warehouses.

They operated the gates.

They were repairing the walls.

They carried goods.

They guarded the mines.

The elves spent a hundred years building a system that worked only because the defeated obeyed its commands.

That night, the defeated people stopped doing them.

The first fights broke out near weapons warehouses.

Then at the gates.

The elven garrison tried to gather in one place, but by the time the commanders realized the scale of the rebellion, part of the city was already beyond their control.

Thorgrim fought in the streets with the Iron Hammers.

For the first time, Entei was no longer just a symbol.

As an elven force tried to retake one of the main gates, its roar echoed through the stone walls of Dur-Garim.

The fire crossed the road.

The dwarves followed him.

Entei did not win the battle for the Iron Hammers.

But wherever he appeared, the dwarves were reminded why they had begun to believe that victory was even possible months earlier.

By dawn, no Vaelthar banner hung over Dur-Gari. Thorgrim stood before the gate leading into the mountain.

Warriors gathered around him.

Some were bleeding.

Others, for the first time in their lives, held weapons that they didn't have to hide from an elven patrol.

Someone started cheering.

Thorgrim turned around.

- Not yet.

The voices fell silent.

“Dur-Garim is free. Khar-Durim does not.

He looked southeast.

Towards Brumwald.

- Let's go get the rest.

Brumwald

Haldrek didn't start out fighting.

He started with warehouses.

Even before the first blow of the dwarven hammer, the Copper Gears knew which granaries they must secure, which roads they must close, and which buildings must not be set on fire, no matter how many elves barricade themselves within them.

Brumwald was the granary of Khar-Durim.

If the uprising was to last longer than a few days, it could not be turned into a disaster.

Haldrek kept telling the Copper Gears:

- We will rebuild the houses. Grain grows slower.

The Copper Gears knew their own mechanisms better than the occupiers who had been using them for a hundred years. The channels were closed.

Others were opened.

The waterwheels stopped exactly when the elves needed them.

A heavy door suddenly fell down in the warehouse that was to be used as a garrison assembly point.

When an elven party tried to cross one of the bridges, they discovered that the mechanism lifting the structure had been activated from the other side.

Haldrek was not going to fight fair.

The honest war was for those who didn't spend a hundred years preparing for the next one.

By noon, Brumwald was under the control of the Copper Gears.

But Haldrek did not celebrate.

There was a more important goal ahead of him.

Port.

It was through him that gold flowed from Khar-Durim for decades.

This was where orders from Sah'Rava arrived.

New soldiers arrived there.

And if Vaelthar was going to send reinforcements, this was where he expected to drop them off.

Haldrek knew that the port had to be captured before the elves understood what was happening on the island.

Not tomorrow.

Not in a week.

Now.

Battle of Port

The elven garrison in the harbor was larger than the one in Brumwald. And unlike the surprised guards in smaller settlements, he had time to prepare.

When the Copper Gears arrived, the gates were closed.

Archers stood on the walls.

The quay was secured.

Haldrek looked at the fortifications.

One of his warriors asked:

- Battering rams?

- NO.

- Ladders?

- NO.

- So how do we get in?

Haldrek pointed to a drainage channel that ran under one part of the harbor.

-We built this place.

For a hundred years the elves have changed the port.

They were expanding it.

They were adding warehouses.

Outposts.

New gates.

They didn't change one thing.

Foundations.

There was still a dwarven drainage system under the streets.

The Copper Gears knew him.

Haldrek divided the warriors.

One group launched a mock attack on the main gate.

The second one disappeared near the canals. The third one was waiting.

The first mechanism stopped working.

Then the second one.

One of the port gates, which the elves thought was closed, suddenly twitched.

It didn't open.

Not yet.

The dwarves beneath the streets have unlocked the old system.

On the surface, another group of Copper Gears reached the mechanism.

The chains started moving.

The gate began to rise.

The elven commander understood what was happening.

Too late.

The Battle of the Port was no longer a revolt of workers against overseers.

For the first time since the beginning of the uprising, two prepared units faced each other.

Elven army.

And a dwarven army.

The Copper Gears entered through their own gate.

Then the usual fight began.

Swords.

Axes.

Shields.

Blood on the stone quay.

Haldrek led the final assault against the building from which the elven commander attempted to direct the defense. When it was all over, he walked out to the harbor.

Vaelthar's banner still hung above the main tower.

One of the dwarves looked at him.

Haldrek nodded.

The banner fell.

After almost a hundred years, the port of Khar-Durim once again belonged to the dwarves.

And it was then that Haldrek looked out to sea.

There was nothing on the horizon yet.

But he knew he would show up.

Vaelthar could ignore minor rebellions.

He couldn't ignore the whole island.

Haldrek sent scouts.

Then he began to prepare the coast.

The North is rising

Meanwhile, far to the north, the elven garrisons had their own problems.

In Kar-Dor, the Stone Shields did exactly what was expected of them.

They closed the door.

Only this time the elves were on the wrong side.

Borgrim remembered the first war.

He remembered how the Stone Shields had closed behind the walls and waited for Vaelthar to come for them.

This time he wasn't going to wait.

Resistance points were isolated. The crossings were cut off.

The dwarves knew every corridor of Kar-Dor.

The elven garrison only knew those they were allowed to walk.

After a few hours the fortress was free.

Borgrim left some warriors to defend it.

He ordered the rest to prepare for the march.

One of the commanders was surprised.

— Are we leaving Kar-Dor?

Borgrim looked at him.

— A hundred years ago we stayed.

He didn't need to add anything more.

In Gor-Dum the fight was different.

The Deep Forges have waited for this day for generations.

When news of the First Forge reached Varkun, he reportedly did not even ask if the news was certain.

He stood up.

He took the gun.

And he said:

—The First Fire is back.

The elves who controlled some of the entrances to Gor-Dum quickly discovered that the city inside the mountain was a very bad place to fight the dwarves that were born there.

The Deep Forges emerged from passages that the occupiers had never marked on maps.

They attacked the posts from several sides.

They cut off the retreat.

They didn't take many prisoners. Varkun made no secret of what he thought of Vaelthar's servants.

When Gor-Dum was reclaimed, some of its warriors wanted to stay.

For a hundred years the elves stood at their gate.

Now they wanted to look after her themselves.

Varkun refused.

— The mountain does not end at our gate.

The Deep Forges moved south.

Stone Shields and Deep Forges met on the eastern route.

There was no big ceremony.

Borgrim looked at Varkun.

Varkun on Borgrim.

Behind them stood two troops who, a hundred years earlier, would probably have returned to their own strongholds after reclaiming their lands.

Borgrim asked:

-Dur-Garim?

—Dur-Garim.

And they set off together.

To the south of them was another elven column.

The soldiers tried to make their way towards the capital, not knowing that Dur-Garim had already fallen.

They saw the Stone Shields first.

Borgrim's heavy infantry occupied the road.

The elves struck.

The shields were durable.

They tried again.

The Stone Shields took a few steps back. Not one more.

Only then did the Deep Forges appear to the side.

Varkun had no intention of standing still.

His warriors rammed into the side of the elven column.

The battle lasted briefly.

Afterwards, Borgrim looked out over the field.

- Too fast.

Varkun wiped the blade.

-Are you complaining?

- NO. I remember.

A hundred years earlier, each of them would have fought alone.

Now one stopped his opponent.

The second one destroyed it.

For the first time, Thorgrim's lesson was no longer just words.

Sails

A few days have passed.

Thorgrim reached the southeast with the Iron Hammers.

When he arrived at the port, the elven banner was no longer there.

Haldrek was waiting on the quay.

Thorgrim looked around at the signs of struggle.

— I was late.

- As usual.

Thorgrim looked at him. Haldrek pointed to the sea.

- But you'll still have time for that.

Sails were appearing on the horizon.

Vaelthar finally answered.

An elven fleet sailed from Sah'Rava.

The soldiers on board expected to enter an empire-controlled port.

Instead of an elven banner, they saw a dwarven one.

The fleet slowed down.

For a moment, Haldrek wondered whether the commander would attempt an assault from the sea.

He didn't try.

The port was prepared.

Entering the narrow bay under dwarven fire would be suicide.

The ships turned.

To the west.

Along the south coast.

Looking for a place to drop off the soldiers.

Thorgrim watched them from the quayside.

- Where to?

Haldrek replied:

— If I were their commander? As far away from us as possible.

- You're not.

— That's why they're still alive.

The dwarves moved along the coast.

The fleet sailed parallel to them. Sometimes she disappeared behind the rocks.

Then she reappeared.

Haldrek knew the south coast.

He knew where the ships might approach.

He also knew where they shouldn't be.

When he saw clouds gathering over the sea in the evening, he stopped his horse.

Thorgrim looked at him.

- What?

Haldrek looked west.

Then to the shoreline.

On the rocks.

And on the old remains of wood washed ashore by the sea.

He smiled.

"I think I know where they'll land."

Wreckage site

The southern coast of Khar-Durim was not a good place for large ships.

There were rocks hidden under the water.

The currents were treacherous.

Even the dwarven captains approached it with caution.

But there were places where smaller craft could get closer to shore.

And above all:

it was far from the port.

The elven commander didn't have many better options.

Haldrek was going to make this one look even better. As night fell, a storm began.

The wind was pounding the coast.

The rain limited visibility.

Ships had to rely on lights from land.

And they saw them.

A few points leading towards what looked from the sea like a safe approach.

Except the lights weren't where they were supposed to be.

The Copper Gears had set them up earlier.

The elven commander saw the way.

Haldrek showed him exactly the one he wanted.

The first ship hit the rocks.

The second one tried to turn.

In the darkness he collided with another one.

Screams were heard on one of the decks.

The lights were moving.

Orders were lost in the wind.

Some of the captains realized that something was wrong and tried to sail away.

The others were too close.

The hulls were cracking.

Ships ran aground.

Smaller boats were lowered into the water.

The soldiers tried to get to the shore.

And then they saw the dwarves. The Iron Hammers struck first.

Thorgrim's warriors waited among the trees and rocks.

The elves getting off the boat didn't have time to form formation.

Entei ran onto one of the exposed rock ledges.

The fire cut through the rain.

The sails of one of the damaged ships burst into flames.

Then another one.

Not all ships sank.

Not all of them were destroyed.

A few managed to turn back.

Haldrek didn't need to destroy the entire fleet.

He just needed to keep her from landing an army on Khar-Durim.

And he achieved it.

In the morning the storm subsided.

There were fragments of wood lying on the shore.

Further on, there were broken hulls stuck on the rocks.

One of the Copper Gears asked:

- Shall we take them apart?

Haldrek looked at the wreckage.

- NO.

- We can get the wood back.

- We have wood.

— Metal.

-We have metal.

The dwarf didn't understand. - So what do we do with them?

Haldrek moved towards the road.

- Nothing. Let them remember where they tried to return.

The wrecks remained.

Over time, trees grew around them.

Four banners

When Thorgrim and Haldrek returned to Dur-Garim, they saw two armies approaching from the northeast.

Stone Shields marched in front.

Behind them, the Deep Forges.

Borgrim and Varkun arrived last.

Not because their creation failed.

They just had the furthest.

In Dur-Garim Square, all four leaders stood together for the first time since the war began.

Thorgrim.

Borgrim.

Haldrek.

Varkun.

Four banners hung above them.

There were warriors from the four parts of the island around.

The Iron Hammers that liberated the capital.

The Copper Gears who captured the port and defeated the fleet.

Stone Shields who left their walls to fight outside them. The Deep Forges, which emerged from the northern mountains for the first time in generations as part of something greater.

Thorgrim looked at the banners.

Then at the gathered dwarves.

—Vaelthar did not defeat Khar-Durim.

There was silence.

- He defeated four clans, one by one.

He pointed to the banners.

“He won't find four this time.”

There was no coronation.

There was no feast.

There was still an elven army in the north.

Vaelthar's last major force on Khar-Durim.

Her commander had already understood something that the king on Sah'Rav still refused to accept.

The occupation could not be saved.

All that was left was to save the soldiers.

Retreat

The elven commander gathered the scattered garrisons and led them north.

He did not try to retake Dur-Garim.

He did not try to regain the port.

He didn't have enough strength.

Most of Vaelthar's army remained on Sah'Rav.

The fleet sent with reinforcements was destroyed.

The four clans marched together. The war for Khar-Durim was lost.

But the elven commander could still do one thing.

Buy time.

On the northern coast, the mountains almost fell into the sea.

There were no wide beaches or ports capable of receiving a large army.

However, there was an escape route.

Lake.

A river flowing from it towards the sea.

Smaller boats could carry soldiers to the coast where larger ships waited.

If the dwarves get there too quickly, the retreat will turn into slaughter.

The elven commander needed several hours.

Maybe a day.

And he knew where he could get them.

To the west of Dur-Garim lay a great gorge.

Wide enough for entire armies to fight in it.

Surrounded by steep slopes.

Leading north.

At its end stood the Gate.

Dwarven.

Monumental.

Older than the elven occupation.

Vaelthar had taken it over a hundred years earlier.

Now his last army would use it against the dwarves who had built it. Thorgrim knew the alternative.

He could have led his army along the eastern route.

She was safer.

Wider.

It allowed us to bypass the gorge.

Haldrek looked at the map.

"If we go this way, they'll have a few days."

Borgrim nodded.

- Sufficiently.

Varkun looked at Thorgrim.

- So we're not going this way.

Thorgrim rolled up the map.

- NO.

He looked west.

—We're going through the Gate.

Gorge

The elves were waiting.

They had time to prepare their positions.

Archers took higher places.

The infantry closed the road.

Makeshift barricades crossed part of the valley.

Behind them, far to the north, was the Gate.

Thorgrim saw her when the dwarven army entered the gorge.

For a hundred years, Vaelthar's soldiers passed through it. It was supposed to end that day.

The Stone Shields stood in the center.

Borgrim passed in front of the front row.

— Today we are not defending the wall.

He punched the shield.

— Today the wall is coming with us.

The first rank raised their shields.

Then the second one.

They set off.

Elvish arrows rained down on them from above.

The Stone Shields moved on.

Slowly.

No spectacular charges.

No screaming.

Step.

Shield.

Step.

Shield.

When the first line reached the elven infantry, it stopped.

And she did what Stone Shields did best.

She didn't budge.

The Iron Hammers and Deep Forges moved in the wings.

Thorgrim led some. Varkun second.

There was no sabotage or surprise here anymore.

The two armies attacked each other.

The elves had a better position.

The dwarves had more warriors.

And for the first time in a hundred years they could afford to use this advantage.

The Copper Gears were slightly behind.

Not because they didn't fight.

Haldrek had another task.

When elven arrows began to fall from one of the slopes, his engineers responded with their own machines.

When a dwarven force needed to pass through a barricade, the Copper Gears dismantled it.

When the wounded began to return from the front line, wagons were waiting behind them.

When the bolts ran out, more crates appeared.

Haldrek had been preparing his army for war for months.

Now he was making her fight for more than an hour.

The battle continued.

The elves were retreating.

They didn't run away.

Their commander knew why he was there.

Each meter of the gorge meant more minutes for the troops evacuated in the north.

He withdrew the soldiers in stages.

One line fought.

The second one continued to prepare the position. Then she was the first to leave.

The dwarves pressed on.

Hour by hour.

Farther and farther north.

Getting closer to the Gate.

Entei fought alongside Thorgrim.

His fire broke the elven formations.

The roar echoed off the gorge walls.

But even he couldn't end the battle with one attack.

The elves were prepared.

They had Pokémon.

They had archers.

They had an area.

This wasn't the legend of one mighty creature destroying an army.

It was a battle of thousands of warriors.

Entei was one of the participants.

The most powerful.

But still only one element of a larger whole.

Retreat.

Krasnoludy ruszyły za nimi.

And then the great wings of the structure began to close.

Stone. Metal.

Chains.

Mechanizmy ukryte w skałach.

Before the dwarven army stood its own Gate.

Closed.

We are not destroying the Gate

Varkun approached first.

He looked at the monumental structure.

- We'll break it down.

Borgrim replied immediately:

— No.

Varkun turned around.

- The elves are running after her.

- I know.

— Every hour—

— I said no.

Thorgrim looked at Borgrim.

The old dwarf placed his hand on the stone.

“This Gate stood here before Vaelthar.

“And now she serves him,” Varkun said.

Borgrim looked at him.

- NO. It serves the one who controls the mechanism.

Haldrek stepped closer. - And the mechanism is controlled by elves.

Borgrim pointed to a side slope.

- For now.

The Stone Shields knew the construction of the Gate.

Not every detail.

For a hundred years the elves have been making changes.

But the basics remained dwarven.

Passages for builders.

Routes that allow you to reach the mechanisms without dismantling the entire structure.

They didn't blow up the entire wall.

Nie rozbijały Bramy.

Old.

Narrow.

Wewnątrz góry

The Deep Forges went in first.

The narrow passage did not allow fighting with large units.

Numbers didn't matter here.

Varkun led his warriors through technical channels.

The elves knew that such passages existed.

However, they did not expect the dwarves to open one of them so quickly.

The first fight broke out on the stairs.

The second one is at the fork.

There was no room for formations.

Shields.

Axes.

Blades.

A stone a few centimeters from the face.

The Deep Forges pressed forward.

If the elves realize that the main attack is coming through the tunnels, they will send soldiers there.

So the Iron Hammers began their assault on the Gate.

Not to get it.

To make it look like they're trying.

Elvish arrows fell from the perches above.

The Copper Gears returned fire.

All the defenders' attention was focused on the front.

Just as Thorgrim wanted. Inside the mountain, Varkun reached the mechanism.

When the last of the defenders fell, one of the dwarves ran to the large lever.

He jerked.

Nothing.

The mechanism did not move.

Varkun cursed.

-Haldrek!

Last opening

Haldrek entered the chamber a few minutes later.

He looked at the wheels.

Chains.

Counterweights.

The old dwarven mechanism was repaired by the elves for a hundred years.

Dotknął jednego z kół.

— Gdzie jest palenisko?

Borgrim replied:

- Below us.

They came down. The old stove was still there.

It hasn't been used for years.

Haldrek examined the wires.

- We can open it.

Thorgrim looked at him.

- Then open it.

- Once.

- What?

- We'll open it once.

Haldrek pointed to the damaged drive.

- Once it starts, we won't stop it without another repair. And part of the mechanism may fall apart.

Borgrim clenched his jaw.

- But the Gate will survive?

Haldrek looked at him.

-If you're lucky.

— I don't believe in luck.

- Then start.

There was one more problem.

The furnace needed temperature.

Huge.

And he needed her immediately.

Thorgrim looked at Haldrek.

Haldrek looked at Thorgrim. They both thought the same thing.

Entei entered the chamber.

He looked at the extinguished fireplace for a moment.

A few months earlier, he was standing in front of another forge.

Then his fire began an uprising.

Now he was to open the way to its end.

Thorgrim placed a hand on his back.

Entei moved towards the furnace.

Fire filled the hearth.

At first nothing happened.

Then the metal began to creak.

Haldrek watched the gauges.

- Still.

Entei roared.

The flame became stronger.

Something hit somewhere above them.

One wheel shook.

Then the second one.

The chain tightened.

Haldrek shouted:

-Now!

The dwarves rushed to the lever.

The mechanism started. Outside, the combatants heard a sound that no living dwarf had heard in generations.

The great chains began to shift.

The stone trembled.

The elves on the walls looked back.

The gate trembled.

Slowly.

Centimeter by centimeter.

It was opening.

Not under elven command.

Under the dwarven.

Borgrim watched as his ancestors' structure fell back into the hands of the dwarves after a hundred years.

Haldrek stared at the mechanism, probably praying to whatever gods he didn't believe in that it would last a few more seconds.

Varkun stood at the entrance to the chamber with a bloody axe.

Stone Shields held the line.

The Iron Hammers were waiting.

Each clan did their part.

The gate opened sufficiently.

Thorgrim raised his weapon.

He didn't need a speech.

He only said:

— Forward.

End of a hundred years

The dwarves passed through the Gate.

The elven rearguard tried to form a last line.

She didn't hold it.

This time Entei didn't have to save his strength for the next day.

He stepped out in front of the Iron Hammers.

Fire struck the elven positions.

Thorgrim followed him.

Varkun and his warriors emerged from the side passages.

The Stone Shields passed through the open Gate.

The Copper Gears left some of the engineers at the mechanism and joined the rest.

The last defense broke.

There was no big battle after that.

There was a chase.

The elves fled north.

The dwarves followed them.

They saw the first boats at the lake.

Some of them were already on the other side.

Others flowed down the river towards the sea.

On the shore, the remaining soldiers waited for their turn.

Not everyone made it.

Thorgrim could have ordered the pursuit to stop.

He didn't do it.

For a hundred years, Vaelthar's soldiers guarded his home.

Now Thorgrim wanted to see the last of them leave Khar-Durim. Some of the elves died.

Some gave up.

Much of it managed to swim away.

The dwarves reached the northern coast late enough to see the larger ships moving away from the shore.

They had no way to catch up with them.

Thorgrim stood by the water.

The other leaders gathered around him.

Borgrim.

Haldrek.

Varkun.

Entei.

Behind them are the warriors of the four clans.

Someone shouted.

Then someone else.

After a moment, the roar of thousands of dwarven voices filled the northern mountains.

After almost a hundred years, the Vaelthar army was no longer on Khar-Durim.

The dwarves were free.

Thorgrim didn't scream.

He watched the ships sail away.

Haldrek stood next to him.

-We won.

Thorgrim was silent.

— Thorgrim.

-Where is he? Haldrek knew who he was asking about.

-Vaelthar?

Thorgrim nodded.

Haldrek looked out at the sea.

- On Sah'Rav.

Thorgrim turned to him.

- He escaped?

- NO.

That word was worse.

Haldrek continued:

“He never came here.

Thorgrim said nothing for a moment.

Happy birthday.

A hundred years of dwarven children were born under elven banners.

For a hundred years, the mines of Khar-Durim filled the treasuries of Sah'Rava.

For a hundred years the dwarves died in rebellion against a king who didn't even consider them important enough to come to the island himself when they finally rose up against him.

Vaelthar stayed in his palace.

He sent soldiers.

He sent a fleet.

He didn't come himself.

Behind Thorgrim, Khar-Durim celebrated.

It was free for the first time in almost a hundred years.

Thorgrim looked south. Across the sea was Sah'Rava.

And an elven king who was still alive.

Haldrek saw his face.

The joy disappeared from his own.

- NO.

Thorgrim looked at him.

— I haven't said anything yet.

- You didn't have to.

Behind them, the dwarves celebrated the end of the war.

The sea lay before them.

And on the other side of him still lived the ruler whom Thorgrim blamed for a hundred years of slavery.

Khar-Durim regained freedom.

Thorgrim wasn't done yet.

After almost a hundred years, the elven banners disappeared from his cities.

At Dur-Garim, barrels were opened and hidden for years on the day of freedom.

In Brumwald, bonfires were lit between mills.

In Kar-Dor, for the first time in generations, guards stood on the walls solely by order of their own clan.

In Gor-Dum the forges worked all night long.

The dwarves sang.

Saws.

They remembered the fallen.

Some didn't even know what celebrating freedom should actually look like.

No one alive has ever done this before.

Thorgrim did not celebrate.

Debt

Later that day, as the last Elven ships disappeared into the northern sea, Thorgrim asked about the ships.

About supplies.

For the number of warriors capable of continuing to fight.

How many days it would take for the army to cross over to Sah'Rava.

Haldrek listened to him for a moment.

Then he said:

— No.

Thorgrim didn't even look up from the map.

-I didn't ask. - I know.

- So why are you answering?

- Because I know what you're thinking.

Thorgrim pushed the map aside.

They looked at each other in silence for a moment.

You could hear singing behind the walls.

Someone was shouting Thorgrim's name.

Someone else Haldrek.

They both ignored them.

“Khar-Durim is free,” Haldrek said.

-Vaelthar is alive.

- It's not our problem anymore.

Thorgrim stood up.

“He was our problem for a hundred years.

“And we just threw his army into the sea.

-His army.

-You won.

- NO.

Haldrek clenched his jaw.

- So what else do you want?

Thorgrim replied without hesitation:

-His.

Thorgrim didn't want Sah'Rava.

He didn't want elven gold.

He didn't want new lands. He had no intention of establishing dwarven garrisons on the southern island or bringing prisoners from there to the mines.

For almost his entire life, he knew only one man who was responsible in his eyes for everything Khar-Durim had become.

Vaelthar.

The king who started the war.

The king who turned the clans into slaves.

A king whose treasuries were filled with dwarven gold for a hundred years.

And a king who, even when the whole island rose up against him, did not see fit to come in person.

Thorgrim looked at Sah'Rava's map for a moment.

Then he said:

“We paid him for a hundred years with gold, iron and blood.

He looked at the others.

— Now we will pay off the last debt.

Varkun smiled.

Haldrek doesn't.

Thorgrim finished:

“And Vaelthar will be the last to pay.”

Four leaders

Varkun didn't need any convincing.

For the Deep Forges, the liberation of Khar-Durim did not mean the end of the war.

It meant that the dwarves finally had the strength to actually finish it.

“We'll sail,” he said.

Haldrek looked at him.

-Of course you'll swim. Varkun raised an eyebrow.

-Do you mind?

-I have a lot of things against me. I don't have all night to replace them.

Varkun laughed.

—The Elven empire lies open before us. Their fleet destroyed. The army is defeated. Vaelthar—

“I don't care about their empire.

Varkun stopped smiling.

Haldrek gestured towards the wall.

Behind it was Khar-Durim.

- I don't care. We got them back.

Varkun replied calmly:

-And they're still alive.

“That's usually how ending a war works.

Borgrim was silent for the longest time.

Of all four leaders, he probably had the most reason to stay.

He remembered the first invasion.

He remembered Khar-Durim's free time.

He lived for almost an entire century only to see the dwarven banner over Kar-Dor again.

He could return to his stronghold.

Rebuild the walls.

Fix the roads.

Make sure what he saw as a young dwarf would never happen again.

Instead he looked at Thorgrim.

-If you say the war isn't over, the Stone Shields will go. Haldrek turned towards him.

-You won't even think about it?

Borgrim replied:

— I've been wondering for a hundred years.

-And?

— A hundred years ago, each of us knew better than the rest.

He looked at Thorgrim.

— I'm not going to repeat that mistake a few days after we managed to fix it.

Haldrek remained.

Thorgrim gave him no order.

He didn't threaten.

He did not remind that he was the leader of the Uprising.

He simply said:

- Stay.

Haldrek looked at him for a moment.

- What?

- Stay on Khar-Durim.

- And you?

-We'll sail.

—Three clans.

- Yes.

Haldrek swore under his breath.

Thorgrim continued:

- Someone has to stay. Brumwald must be secured. Rebuild the port. The roads are destroyed. If we don't come back— - Shut up.

Thorgrim fell silent.

Haldrek took a few steps.

He looked at Borgrim.

By Varkun.

By Thorgrim.

Just a few days earlier, the four clans had stood side by side in Dur-Garim for the first time in a century.

They passed through the Gate together.

Together they won.

Now three were about to sail away.

One thing to stay.

Haldrek knew that Thorgrim was truly giving him a choice.

And that's why the choice was so difficult.

He could have stayed.

No one would call him a coward.

He captured the port.

He wrecked the fleet.

He fought in the Gorge.

He did more for the freedom of Khar-Durim than most dwarves will ever be able to say about themselves.

But if three clans set out without the fourth, the first rift would appear.

Small.

Perhaps harmless.

But Haldrek had been building machines all his life.

He knew what a small crack could do if allowed to work long enough.

He looked at Thorgrim. - Damn you.

Thorgrim replied:

- Are you swimming?

Haldrek sighed.

- I'm swimming.

Not because he believed in revenge.

Not because he stopped considering the expedition a mistake.

It flowed because after a hundred years of divisions, Khar-Durim had just learned to be one nation.

He wasn't going to be the first to divide them again.

Valoria

The news also reached Valoria.

King Aldrin IV received word that Thorgrim was preparing a fleet and intended to ferry his entire army to Sah'Rava.

Cedric Varen reportedly asked:

- What do we answer?

Aldrin read the letter again.

- Nothing.

"Thorgrim may take silence as consent."

- He doesn't need my consent.

“Vaelthar may take silence as support.

Aldrin put the letter aside.

“Vaelthar accepted many things.

Cedric looked at the king for a moment.

- So we remain neutral?

— Khar-Durim is free. Aldrin stood up.

— We helped them regain their own home. What they do with the elves now is none of Valoria's business.

-We don't condemn?

- NO.

-We don't help?

- NO.

Cedric nodded.

It was a position he understood perfectly.

Valoria did not give the dwarves a single soldier.

She didn't give any ships.

She did not provide food.

But she also did not send a warning to Sah'Rava.

Aldrin simply looked away.

The sea

A few days later, the dwarven ships left Khar-Durim.

For the first time in almost a hundred years, they did not leave port under Elvish supervision.

There were warriors from all four clans on board.

Iron Hammers.

Stone Shields.

Copper Gears.

Deep Forges.

Entei traveled on Thorgrim's ship.

Haldrek stood at the side of his own ship and spent most of the first day staring at the island as it receded.

One of the Copper Gears approached him. -We'll be back.

Haldrek looked at him.

- Is this an order or a prediction?

The dwarf smiled nervously.

- Hope.

Haldrek looked at Khar-Durim again.

- At least that's fair.

Sah'Rava lay to the southeast.

The sea was getting warmer every day.

When the earth appeared on the horizon, the first thing they saw was green.

Jungle.

The western part of Sah'Rava.

Thorgrim did not order banners to be set up on the captured beaches.

He did not build fortifications.

He did not appoint a governor.

He only asked:

-Where is Vaelthar?

Zashara say no

Vaelthar's first order reached Zashar faster than the dwarven army.

An elven emissary arrived at their settlement and demanded warriors.

He didn't ask.

The elven empire rarely asked.

Zashara was supposed to send a unit.

He was to join the army defending the Citadel. Their leader, Rassak, listened to the message until the end.

Then he replied:

— No.

The messenger didn't understand for a moment.

- This is the king's order.

- I know.

-Vaelthar demands-

- I heard.

Rassak looked towards the north, where a dwarven army was landing somewhere beyond the forests.

“When you sailed to their mountains, you took our warriors.

The elf clenched his jaw.

Rassak finished:

— Now the mountains have come for you. This time we stay at home.

The Zashara did not join Thorgrim.

They offered no warriors.

They did not pledge friendship to the dwarves.

When the army from Khar-Durim reached their lands, Rassak met them.

Thorgrim stopped the procession.

The two leaders looked at each other for a moment.

Rassak pointed to a path through the jungle.

-The citadel is over there.

Thorgrim nodded.

-We won't disturb you.

- Neither do we.

That was enough. The dwarves passed through the lands of Zashara.

The lizard people returned to their homes.

One way

Thorgrim did not lead the conquest of Sah'Rava.

He led the march.

Elvish outposts in his path were attacked.

Those that were far away from her remained untouched.

When scouts reported an elven settlement several hours south, Varkun looked at Thorgrim.

"We could get her."

"Is Vaelthar there?"

- NO.

- So let's move on.

- There are elves there.

Thorgrim stopped.

- I know.

Varkun was silent for a moment.

—For a hundred years—

Thorgrim interrupted:

“For a hundred years, Vaelthar has taken time away from us and we will never get it back.

He looked towards the road.

"I won't give him another day."

The elven army tried to delay the march.

One bridge was destroyed. The Copper Gears built a crossing next to it.

The road through the hills was closed.

The Deep Forges purified it.

Archers tried to stop the column at the river.

The Stone Shields carried the rest of the army through the barrage.

The Iron Hammers moved on.

Not every fight deserved a name.

Not all of them later made it into the chronicles.

The dwarves simply moved east.

Each time the elves relented, Thorgrim asked the same question.

-The citadel?

And every time the answer was:

- Next.

Citadel

Finally the jungle ended.

A huge crevice opened up in front of the dwarves.

There was water far below.

The savannah began on the opposite shore.

There was only one road between the two lands.

Stone bridge.

And above it stood the Citadel of Vaelthar.

She wasn't one castle.

She was the whole complex.

On the western side there were walls, gates, towers and barracks. A bridge connected it to the savannah side of the Citadel proper.

There were courtyards there.

Royal halls.

Palace.

And a sanctuary dedicated to Xerneas.

For generations, anyone wishing to pass between the western and central Sah'Rava had to pass under the shadow of elven authority.

Thorgrim looked at the keep.

- There?

The scout nodded.

-Vaelthar is inside.

For the first time since leaving Khar-Durim, Thorgrim smiled.

Request

Before the siege began, Thorgrim sent an envoy.

He did not demand Sah'Rava's surrender.

He didn't ask for gold.

He did not demand territory.

The message was short.

"Render Vaelthar and the dwarven army will return to Khar-Durim."

The elven commander who received the messenger asked:

-Only the king?

- Only him.

- And will you leave?

"That is Thorgrim's order."

The message reached Vaelthar. The king reportedly laughed.

- He crossed the sea for one elf?

One of the advisors replied:

-Your Highness...

Vaelthar looked at him.

- What?

The advisor hesitated.

- They all swam.

Vaelthar refused.

Not just because he was king.

Not only because its release would mean the end of power.

He simply did not believe that former slaves could truly take over the place from which he had ruled Sah'Rava for so many years.

Khar-Durim udało się zbuntować.

Flota poniosła klęskę.

Armia została wyrzucona z wyspy.

Vaelthar saw this as a series of mistakes by his commanders.

Nie dowód, że sam się mylił.

Cytadela była jego domem.

His stronghold.

His symbol.

Nie zamierzał uciekać przed krasnoludami.

Western wall

The first assault began at dawn. Krasnoludy uderzyły na zachodnią część kompleksu.

There was no fast marching here anymore.

Elfy wiedziały, że za nimi znajduje się Vaelthar.

Entei fought alongside Thorgrim.

On the first day, the dwarves captured the outer wall.

On the second, part of the barracks.

On the third, the elves withdrew from the last large tower on the western side of the rift.

They didn't get far.

Behind them was a bridge.

And the main Citadel.

Haldrek climbed the captured wall.

He looked at the stone crossing.

It was wide.

But not enough for the dwarves to take full advantage of their numerical advantage.

On the other side, the elves were preparing barricades.

Archers occupied the towers.

Thorgrim stood next to him. -We'll get through.

Haldrek looked at him.

- Yes.

-You don't sound convincing.

— Because I only want to go through it once.

Bridge

A direct charge would be a massacre.

Haldrek refused.

The Copper Gears spent several hours preparing mobile shields.

Wood.

Metal plates.

Wheels.

Simple structures that could be moved in front of attacking troops.

Borgrim watched the first one.

- Ugly.

Haldrek replied:

- Shield too.

—The shield has dignity.

- This one has a roof.

Borgrim considered.

- Point for you.

The Stone Shields moved first.

Shields of Copper Gears were moved above and in front of them.

Elvish arrows struck wood and metal. Pokémon were attacking structures.

The Copper Gears repaired them almost as they walked.

When one burned, it was moved aside and the next one was pushed through.

As the first line of Stone Shields reached the barricade, the Iron Hammers struck through the prepared gap.

Potem kolejny metr.

I następny.

The bridge became the bloodiest place of the entire siege.

There was nowhere to avoid the enemy.

There was no wide field.

There was a stone road over a precipice.

Przód.

Back.

And death between them.

The elves knew there was a palace behind them.

The dwarves knew that Vaelthar was behind the elves.

Nobody wanted to give in.

At one point, one of the elven barricades burst into flames.

Not from Entei.

From the defenders' own fire.

Smoke filled the bridge.

Thorgrim looked at Entei.

He didn't say anything.

The Pokémon moved.

He ran through the curtain of smoke. There were screams on the other side.

The Iron Hammers followed him.

The first line broke.

Then the second one.

The elves began to retreat towards the eastern entrance to the Citadel.

The dwarves crossed the bridge.

Inside

After the bridge, everything changed.

There was no longer one front line.

The citadel had dozens of corridors.

Courtyards.

Stairs.

Halls.

Smaller gates.

Passages leading to other parts of the complex.

After several hours of fighting, the four clans were still pursuing one plan, but their commanders had lost sight of each other.

Thorgrim advanced towards the main palace.

Varkun tried to capture more inner courtyards.

Borgrim secured the passages so that the elves could not cut off the troops beyond.

Haldrek was tasked with opening one of the side gates leading to the inner part of the Citadel.

The Copper Gears took a different route.

Haldrek did not know where exactly Vaelthar was. Nobody knew anymore.

Each captured elf said something different.

The king is in the sanctuary.

The king is in the throne room.

The king left the Citadel.

The king leads the defense.

The king escaped.

Haldrek stopped asking.

He had his job.

They crossed the narrow courtyard.

Then through the gallery partially destroyed during the shelling.

One of the gates was closed.

The Copper Gears opened it.

Behind her was a long corridor.

Much richer than the previous ones.

Sculptures.

Decorations.

Xerneas's motives.

And almost no soldiers.

Haldrek stopped the squad.

- There's something I don't like here.

One of the dwarves looked ahead.

— Are we going back?

Haldrek sighed.

— If I came back every time I didn't like something, I'd still be in Brumwald. They moved on.

At the end of the corridor they found a large hall.

And Vaelthar.

King

The elven king did not look like the ruler of an empire that was falling apart.

He didn't run away.

He wasn't injured.

He didn't beg the guards for a way out.

He stood in the middle of his own room, fully armed.

Behind it were tall windows.

Symbols of the elven monarchy on the walls.

Haldrek stopped.

Vaelthar looked at the dwarves.

Then to Haldrek.

"Thorgrim?"

Haldrek shook his head.

- NO.

- Pity.

-For him more than for you.

Haldrek turned to one of the Copper Gears.

-Find Thorgrim.

The dwarf nodded.

Vaelthar noticed the gesture. - Will you wait?

Haldrek looked at him.

- This is his war.

Vaelthar laughed.

- NO.

He looked at Haldrek's bloody hammer.

"Since you came here first, she's obviously yours."

Haldrek didn't answer.

Vaelthar took a step forward.

“For a hundred years your people have dreamed of seeing me dead.

— My main dream was that you would leave us alone.

- And yet you are in my house.

Haldrek tightened his grip on the hammer.

“You can thank Thorgrim for that, too.”

Vaelthar looked at the remaining dwarves.

- How many of you do you need?

Haldrek frowned.

-For what?

- To kill one elf.

Some of the Copper Gears moved forward.

Haldrek raised his hand.

They stopped.

“Don't do that,” one of them said.

Haldrek did not look away from Vaelthar.

— If we attack together, he'll tell the afterlife that we needed the whole squad. - I don't care what he says.

- Me neither.

Haldrek placed his other hand on the handle of his hammer.

- But he cares.

Vaelthar smiled.

Haldrek stepped out in front of his own unit.

And they started.

Duel

Vaelthar was faster.

Haldrek understood this after the first few blows.

The Elven king was not a ruler who sat solely on the throne for a hundred years.

He fought before.

He trained.

He was a better swordsman than most of the opponents Haldrek faced during the Uprising.

The hammer had strength.

Sword speed.

Vaelthar exploited this mercilessly.

Haldrek tried to close the distance.

Vaelthar was moving away.

The dwarf struck.

The elf avoided.

The sword sliced through Haldrek's side. Then the arm.

The Copper Gears watching the duel began to realize that something was wrong.

Haldrek too.

But he wasn't going to stop.

-Is this who you chose? Vaelthar asked between blows.

Haldrek parried the blow.

- What?

- War.

- NO.

The hammer sliced ​​through the air inches from Vaelthar's head.

“That's what Thorgrim chose.

Vaelthar laughed.

-And you swam after him.

Haldrek struck again.

- Yes.

- So what's the difference?

Haldrek didn't answer for a moment.

— I know when to stop.

Vaelthar attacked.

This time Haldrek didn't make it.

The sword went deep under the armor.

The dwarf stepped back.

Vaelthar snatched the blade away.

Haldrek fell to one knee. There was silence in the room.

One of the Copper Gears moved.

Haldrek raised his hand.

He stopped him.

Vaelthar watched.

Blood flowed down Haldrek's armor.

The elven king knew where he was going.

He knew the fight was over.

— It's over.

Haldrek didn't answer.

He rested the hammer on the floor.

He tried to get up.

It didn't work.

Vaelthar turned around.

There was the sound of metal sliding behind him.

Vaelthar looked over his shoulder.

Haldrek tried to get up again.

This time he stopped.

Wobbly.

He held onto the wound with one hand.

The second hammer.

Vaelthar looked at him in disbelief.

— Why are you still standing?

Haldrek looked at the elven king. He took a breath.

- Because you're still standing.

First strike

Vaelthar managed to raise his sword.

He didn't have time to avoid the hammer.

Haldrek no longer tried to fight quickly.

He had no strength.

He didn't have time.

He only has a few strokes left.

The first hit Vaelthar in the chest.

The metal of the king's armor bent.

The plate broke.

Vaelthar took a few steps back.

For the first time since the beginning of the duel, the smile disappeared from his face.

Second strike

Haldrek followed him.

Every step left blood on the floor.

Vaelthar tried to regain ground.

The sword cut through the air.

Haldrek took a blow to his armor.

He didn't stop.

The hammer struck a second time.

Lower. Vaelthar lost his balance.

He fell to his knees.

The sword fell from his hand.

Haldrek stood over him.

Barely.

Vaelthar looked up.

Perhaps he wanted to say something.

Perhaps for the first time in his life he had nothing to say.

This was never established.

Third strike

Haldrek raised his hammer.

And he struck for the third time.

Vaelthar fell.

He didn't get up.

For a moment, no one in the room moved.

Haldrek stood over the dead king.

Then he dropped the hammer.

The weapon hit the stone.

The dwarf staggered.

Copper Gears got to him before he fell.

Too late

Thorgrim ran into the hall a few minutes later.

Behind him is Entei and some of the Iron Hammers.

He saw Vaelthar first.

Dead.

Then Haldrek.

Leaning on one of his warriors.

The pallor of his face spoke more than the wound.

Thorgrim stopped.

He looked at Vaelthar's body for several seconds.

He had been waiting for this sight his whole life.

He had imagined it hundreds of times.

He never imagined that he would be standing a few meters away while someone else did it for him.

He approached Haldrek.

- This was supposed to be my duel.

Haldrek opened his eyes.

He looked at him.

— We should have gone faster.

Thorgrim let out a short laugh.

Perhaps the only one he could afford at the time.

Then he looked back at Vaelthar.

- You killed him.

Haldrek closed his eyes.

-Apparently.

Thorgrim sat down next to him.

The battle was still going on all around. There were sounds of fighting in the distance.

Screaming.

Metal.

Orders.

However, no one fought in this one room anymore.

Haldrek spoke after a moment.

-Tell Eldric...

He fell silent.

Thorgrim waited.

Haldrek opened his eyes.

- NO.

- What?

- You'll tell him yourself.

Thorgrim looked at him.

Haldrek smiled weakly.

- After all, it was your idea.

Thorgrim did not answer.

After a few minutes, Haldrek stopped breathing.

Thorgrim stayed with him a moment longer.

On one side lay the man he had hated all his life.

On the other side, the dwarf who had told him from the beginning that he shouldn't come here.

They were both dead.

Thorgrim got exactly what he wanted.

Vaelthar was dead. Only the revenge he had waited his whole life for was not what he had imagined.

That same day, the story spread throughout the Citadel.

Not about the entire siege.

Not about the bridge.

Not the three days of fighting for the western walls.

About three strikes.

The first to crumble the royal armor.

The second that brought Vaelthar to his knees.

And the third one that ended his reign.

Over time, the dwarven chronicles will record:

With the first he crushed his armor. With the second he brought the king to his knees. With the third he ended a hundred years of captivity.

Haldrek never heard these words.

He'd probably roll his eyes at them anyway.

Vaelthar was dead.

The Elven empire still existed.

At least for the next few hours.

Because the death of one king does not end history just because someone struck the hammer a third time.

Sometimes it's only then that it really starts.
