chronicles-story-6.content:
Vaelthar was dead.

@@LORE_IMAGE:chronicles-story-6@@

For the first few minutes, almost no one except those in his room knew about it.

Fighting continued in other parts of the Citadel.

The elves defended the stairs.

The dwarves captured more courtyards.

Orders were still given on the walls in the name of the king, who lay dead on the stone floor.

Thorgrim sat next to Haldrek.

He no longer looked at Vaelthar.

He looked at the dwarf who had told him from the beginning that they shouldn't come here.

Haldrek was also dead.

Thorgrim got exactly what he came to Sah'Rava for.

He didn't feel like a winner.

The king is dead

The news came out of the room faster than any order. First the Copper Gears knew.

Then the Iron Hammers.

Someone said it in the courtyard.

Someone else repeated at the west gate.

The elven soldier heard the words spoken in Dwarvish and asked what they meant.

Another elf answered him.

-Vaelthar is dead.

At first no one believed it.

Then there was no king to deny it.

The elven defense did not crumble in an instant.

Some continued to fight.

Out of loyalty.

Out of fear.

Out of anger.

Or simply because they were facing armed dwarves and had no time to think about the future of the empire.

But something has changed.

The orders began to trail off.

The commanders asked who now had the right to issue them.

Some troops retreated to the eastern part of the Citadel.

Others laid down their weapons.

Still others simply tried to get out of the compound.

The state, which for decades had been based on the will of one king, suddenly found itself without his will.

It took the dwarves three days to capture the western fortifications.

Another few hours to cross the bridge. After Vaelthar's death, the rest of the Citadel began to fall much faster.

Thorgrim only left the hall when Haldrek's body was taken away.

Varkun was waiting in the courtyard.

There was dried blood on his armor.

- That's true?

Thorgrim nodded.

-Vaelthar is dead.

Varkun spojrzał w stronę wschodnich murów.

Then he smiled.

— Więc teraz możemy skończyć.

Thorgrim stopped.

- We're done.

Varkun odwrócił głowę.

- What?

-Vaelthar is dead.

- I know.

“We came for him.

- You swam for him.

They looked at each other in silence for a moment.

Around them, dwarves led prisoners.

Somewhere further away, a part of the palace was burning.

“Their army is broken,” Varkun said. - They don't have a king. The citadel is ours. If we move now, no one can stop us.

Thorgrim did not answer.

Varkun took a step closer. — They stood in our cities for a hundred years.

- I know.

“They made us work for themselves for a hundred years.

- I know.

— They killed our people.

Thorgrim looked at him.

—I said I knew.

Varkun pointed towards the east.

"So why are they still there?"

Where does revenge end?

Varkun was not a madman.

He knew exactly what he wanted.

The Elven state was weaker than ever.

The three great houses have long argued over Vaelthar's policies.

The subjugated peoples of Sah'Rava were only waiting for a sign that the crown could no longer punish them.

If the dwarves marched on, they could destroy what remained of the elven power.

Perhaps forever.

For Varkun, this was why Groudon allowed them to survive a hundred years of captivity.

So that one day they can make sure it never happens again.

“We don't have to enslave them,” he said. “We don't need their lands.

Thorgrim was silent.

“All we have to do is make sure they're never a threat again.

- How?

Varkun replied without hesitation, "We will destroy their armies."

- And then?

- We will disarm the settlements.

- And then?

— We will destroy those who try to rebuild it.

- And then?

Varkun frowned.

Thorgrim took a step towards him.

- What about the children of these soldiers?

Varkun didn't say anything.

— If in twenty years they take up arms, will we kill them too?

—If they threaten Khar-Durim—

- And their children?

Varkun clenched his jaw.

Thorgrim looked at him.

— Where does your revenge end, Varkun?

Varkun did not answer.

Thorgrim could.

— Mine ends there.

He pointed towards the room where Vaelthar lay.

- He's dead.

- And the others?

“The others are not Vaelthar.

“They guarded our mines.

- Some. — They took our gold.

- Some.

— They took advantage of our captivity.

Thorgrim was silent for a moment.

"And how many of them will we kill before you think enough is enough?"

Varkun did not answer.

-Ten?

Silence.

- Thousand?

Silence.

- All of them?

Varkun looked Thorgrim in the eyes.

And this time it was Thorgrim who understood the answer first.

- NO.

Varkun shook his head.

—Thorgrim—

“We didn't throw off their shackles to learn how to forge them.

— Nobody talks about shackles.

- Still.

Thorgrim looked at the Citadel.

“Vaelthar didn't sail to Khar-Durim and say on the first day that his soldiers would still be watching over our children a hundred years later.

Varkun snorted.

- Are you comparing us to him?

Thorgrim replied calmly:

- Not yet. That word hurt more than the accusation.

Varkun was silent for a long moment.

Finally he asked:

- What if they come back?

- Then we will fight.

- And we will wait again until they arrive at our gates?

- NO.

Thorgrim looked at him.

— This time Khar-Durim is one kingdom.

“It could be something bigger.

- I don't want a bigger one.

- I want a safe one.

Thorgrim nodded.

- Me too. That's why we're going home.

Varkun did not kneel.

He didn't apologize.

He didn't say Thorgrim was right.

He just left.

The Deep Forges obeyed their king's orders.

But in Gor-Dum it will be said for many years to come that on that day Thorgrim stopped the dwarven army one victory too early.

Three answers

Vaelthar's death ended one question. Who is the king of Sah'Rava?

The answer was:

nobody.

But immediately another one appeared.

Who should become it?

The elven families did not need time to find candidates.

They needed something much more difficult.

Common answer to the question:

why did Vaelthar lose?

They couldn't find her.

Vyrn

The most radical were gathered around House Vyrn.

For them, the tragedy was not the invasion of Khar-Durim.

It wasn't even slavery.

The tragedy was that Vaelthar could not hold on to what he had gained.

He allowed the dwarves to keep their clans.

He allowed them to remember past leaders.

He allowed them to preserve their language, traditions and the belief that the mountains still belonged to them.

And when the Uprising broke out, he didn't even consider it worthy of his own presence.

For House Vyrn, Vaelthar did not lose because he was too brutal.

He lost because he turned out to be too weak at the decisive moment.

If it were up to them, the future elven state would never again allow its subjects to maintain the strength needed to rebel.

The other houses listened to them and saw the exact same path that led the Citadel to ruins. They weren't going to go down it.

Aelthir

House Aelthir came to the opposite conclusion.

Vaelthar did not lose the war.

He lost a decision made before it even started.

Before the invasion, Khar-Durim was a wealthy, sometimes irritating, sometimes inconvenient neighbor.

After the invasion, it became a nation waiting for a hundred years for the opportunity to take revenge.

The empire had to maintain garrisons.

Fleet.

Supervisors.

Transport.

Outposts.

And the entire system of coercion needed to control a people who never wanted to be controlled.

For a hundred years, Sah'Rava paid for Vaelthar's decision.

In the end, she also paid with Vaelthar himself.

For Aelthir the conclusion was simple:

Khar-Durim should never have been sailed.

They didn't want another empire built on occupation.

They also did not want another war to regain their former power.

They wanted to survive what was left of it.

The Vyrn called it cowardice.

They called Aelthir memory.

Silvar

The most complicated answer belonged to the Silvar family.

Of all the houses, they were most closely associated with the ancient teachings of Xerneas.

They talked about balance.

About harmony.

About the duty of the stronger and wiser towards those who do not understand the world order.

They condemned slavery.

They condemned the massacres.

They condemned the occupation of Khar-Durim.

However, this did not mean that they stopped considering elves as a special people.

According to them, Vaelthar confused leadership with dominion.

There was no need to capture the dwarven cities.

It was enough to control trade.

There was no need to take away their leaders.

It was possible to play four clans against each other.

There was no need to put on shackles.

Khar-Durim could be made self-dependent on Elven ports, markets, and support.

For Silvar, slavery was not the goal.

The goal was to create a world in which others willingly - or at least without a sword at their throat - follow wherever the elves direct.

Some called it wiser policy.

Others:

the better-named belief that elves still have the right to decide for everyone else.

Three houses could agree on one thing.

Vaelthar was dead. Their agreement ended on everything else.

Vyrn wanted to rebuild his empire stronger than before.

Aelthir wanted to leave the empire in the past.

Silvar wanted to regain elven influence, but without the sword and chains.

They couldn't even agree on what the new kingdom would be.

That's why it wasn't created.

Each family retreated to their own lands.

Everyone took their supporters with them.

Everyone kept their own version of events.

The crown of Vaelthar was left without an heir.

Not because no one wanted her.

Because no one agreed on what else it should mean.

End of tributes

However, the elves were not the only ones who heard the news of Vaelthar's death.

There were peoples on Sah'Rav for whom the words:

"The King is Dead"

they meant something completely different.

The goblin emissary apparently reached his settlement in the evening.

Tired.

Covered in dust.

He entered through the stockade.

Someone asked:

- Yeah? The Messenger replied:

-Vaelthar is dead.

There was silence for a few seconds.

Then someone brought a barrel.

No one knows who.

The next day, no one worked in the goblin settlement.

Bonfires were burning.

Ate.

Drank.

There was dancing.

Someone apparently tried to burn an elven tribute register, but it turned out that it was too thick and burned very badly.

Eventually it was used to start a larger fire.

The Sah'Rava council was not convened.

No envoys were sent to the three elven houses.

They were not asked who would be the next king.

They simply stopped paying.

That was enough for the goblins.

Zashara

The Zashara had even less to say.

They had already denied Vaelthar warriors.

When they learned of his death, they did not organize a big celebration.

Rassak listened to the message.

He nodded. And the next day, life in the settlement was almost the same as before.

They were hunted.

Houses were repaired.

Children were running between the trees.

Someone was tending the crops.

No one came for tribute.

No one demanded warriors.

This was all the revolution the Zashara needed.

Nekhari

The Nekhari reacted differently.

In the desert, memory lasted longer.

Time didn't take it away from them as quickly as it did from others.

There were still those in Nekhara who remembered the stories of the warriors sent to Khar-Durim a hundred years earlier.

Some might even remember the warriors themselves.

Therefore, after Vaelthar's death, they did not limit themselves to removing elven symbols.

They sent a message.

Thorgrim met Nekhari while preparing to leave Sah'Rava.

The dwarven ships were almost ready.

Haldrek's body was waiting for a ship to take it to Brumwald.

Several desert dwellers stood before the king.

Their costumes were ceremonial.

They had no weapons.

The oldest of them bowed his head. — King Khar-Durim.

Thorgrim wasn't used to this title yet.

- Speak.

The Nekhara messenger replied:

— A hundred years ago, our warriors came to your island.

Thorgrim looked at him without saying a word.

—They fought alongside Vaelthar.

- I know.

— They didn't come there willingly.

Thorgrim narrowed his eyes.

- Is that supposed to be an excuse?

- NO.

The answer came immediately.

- Explanation.

The Nekhari told about the tributes.

About threats.

What Vaelthar did to the peoples of Sah'Rava when they refused to comply with his demands.

But at the end the emissary said something that Thorgrim had not expected.

— They were our hands.

He fell silent.

- Although the order was his.

He didn't say:

we are not guilty.

He didn't say: we had no choice.

He didn't ask Thorgrim to forget.

He only admitted that Vaelthar gave the order and the Nekhari carried it out.

—We are sorry for what we did on Khar-Durim.

Thorgrim was silent for a long time.

Finally the emissary added:

- And thank you.

- What for?

— For never having to obey such an order again.

Thorgrim looked towards the Citadel.

Then back to Nekhari.

-Vaelthar is dead.

-We know.

- So we don't have anything else to talk about.

The messenger bowed his head.

For Thorgrim, that was all the answer.

For Nekhari it was enough.

Back

The dwarves left Sah'Rava the same way they came.

They left no garrisons.

They did not collect tributes.

They did not set boundaries.

They didn't take land.

The ruins of the Citadel were left behind. Just like the three elven families who were just starting to build three different versions of the future.

As the army passed through Zashar's lands again, Rassak was waiting by the road.

There was no feast.

There was no message.

There was no oath of friendship.

Thorgrim marched in front.

Rassak looked at him.

Then he bowed his head.

Only once.

Thorgrim stopped.

He responded with the same gesture.

And he went further.

Neither of them said a word.

There was no need for this.

Ships were waiting on the coast.

Four clans sailed to Sah'Rava.

Four were coming back.

But not four leaders.

Haldrek returned to Khar-Durim in a closed coffin.

There were still traces of his last fight on his hammer.

The Copper Gears did not sing on the first day of their journey.

Neither did Thorgrim. Borgrim found him on deck in the evening.

The king looked at the sea.

— Do you regret it? Borgrim asked.

Thorgrim did not answer immediately.

—Vaelthar had to die.

Borgrim nodded.

— That's not what I asked.

Thorgrim looked at him.

The old dwarf did not repeat the question.

He didn't have to.

After a long while, Thorgrim said:

—If I had stayed on Khar-Durim, Haldrek would have lived.

- Maybe.

"Vaelthar too."

- Yes.

Thorgrim looked out to sea again.

— I don't know if I would have chosen otherwise.

Borgrim replied:

- That's good.

Thorgrim frowned.

- All right?

— If after everything you were sure that every decision you made was right, I would start to fear you.

Borgrim is gone.

Thorgrim was left alone.

Iron Crown

Crowds were waiting for Khar-Durim.

News of Vaelthar's death arrived before the fleet.

So does the story of Haldrek.

There were cheers every time the ship returned.

Then the dwarves saw the coffin.

And some of the voices fell silent.

Thorgrim returned victorious.

Vaelthar was dead.

The Elven empire has fallen.

Khar-Durim was free.

No elven king gave orders in his mines anymore.

No ships left the port with tribute to Sah'Rava.

No dwarven guard had to watch over his own kin for a foreign lord.

After almost a hundred years, everything that generations of dwarves had wanted had come true.

Yet one more coffin than should have returned to Brumwald.

Eldrik stood among the Copper Gears when she was brought.

Thorgrim approached him.

For a moment neither of them spoke.

The king had his words ready.

About courage.

About the duel.

About Haldrek killing Vaelthar. About the fact that he saved perhaps thousands of dwarves from another war.

That his name will be remembered as long as Khar-Durim exists.

He looked at Eldrik.

And he didn't say any of them.

“I didn't tell him to swim.

Eldrik looked at him.

- I know.

Thorgrim seemed surprised for a moment.

Eldrik continued:

"You just knew he wouldn't let you sail without him."

Thorgrim found no answer.

Eldrik turned towards the coffin.

The conversation is over.

Not a conflict.

After the war

Khar-Durim did not become one nation because four clans suddenly began to agree with each other.

The Iron Hammers believed that Thorgrim had done what had to be done.

The Stone Shields trusted the king who had reclaimed their homeland.

The Copper Gears returned to Brumwald without Haldrek.

The Deep Forges returned to Gor-Dum with the belief that the war had ended just when it was just starting to get really interesting.

No one left the kingdom.

No one started another rebellion.

The four banners still stood side by side.

But unity no longer meant that everyone thought the same. Maybe she never meant it.

On Valoria, Aldrin IV received the news of Vaelthar's death without much ceremony.

He didn't declare war.

He didn't have to sign the peace.

The Elvish king, whom he increasingly feared, ceased to exist.

The balance he was striving for had been achieved.

Years later, he would die of natural causes, convinced that his decisions saved Valoria from war.

His daughter, Elara II, will take the throne.

On Sah'Rav, no one will replace Vaelthar.

Vyrn will remember the empire and dream of the power he believed the last king lacked.

Aelthir will remember the cost of one unnecessary invasion.

Silvar will still speak of Xerneas, harmony, and the elven duty to lead others - though no longer through chains.

The Nekhari will return to the desert.

Goblins to their fires.

Zashara to the jungle.

Each of them will live without the elven collector standing at the gate.

What's left

After wars, there are always more than winners and losers.

A wreck site remained on Khar-Durim.

Over time, trees will grow between the hulls of Elven ships.

The Gate remained. It will still stand at the end of the western gorge, although its mechanism will still bear traces of its last opening for a long time.

The First Forge remained.

Her fire will not be extinguished again.

The Citadel remained on Sah'Rav.

No one will fully rebuild it.

Some of the towers will collapse.

In others, plants will grow.

The bridge between the jungle and the savannah will still lead through the ruins of the place from which almost all of Eryndor was once ruled.

Somewhere inside there will remain a room.

The place where two leaders died.

One that began a hundred years of slavery.

And the second one, who from the very beginning believed that it was not worth going to war during which he ended it.

Years will pass.

Grass will cover the battlefields.

New boards will replace the old ones in the ports.

Children born after the war will not remember the elven guards in Khar-Durim.

The young inhabitants of Sah'Rava will know Vaelthar mainly from the stories of their elders.

History will begin to turn into legend.

Legend into politics.

Politics in an argument at the table.

The dwarven chronicler will write that Thorgrim liberated Khar-Durim and avenged a hundred years of captivity. The elf will write that a dwarven army invaded Sah'Rava and killed its last king.

The Nekhar scholar will recall that for his people, the death of the same king meant freedom.

Copper Tooth may respond that none of these stories will return Haldrek to his son.

Everyone will tell the truth.

At least part of it.

Today, Thorgrim the Iron Crown still rules over Khar-Duri.

The four clans still stand under one banner.

Valoria is ruled by Elara II.

Sah'Rava still has no king.

The war is over.

Not because everyone forgave each other.

Not because all wrongs have been righted.

It wasn't because the people of Eryndor suddenly started looking at the past the same way.

One army just came home one day.

And no one else set off.

This is how the elven empire ended.

Not in one hit.

Not one battle.

Not even the death of one king.

It fell because after his death there was nothing left to force all the peoples of Sah'Rava - or even all the elves - to move in the same direction.

Khar-Durim regained freedom.

Sah'Rava regained her choice. Valoria kept her peace.

None of these gifts were free.

And not one of the inhabitants of Eryndor forgot the price.

chronicles-peoples.content:
The three great islands of Eryndor differ from each other not only in landscape.

@@LORE_IMAGE:chronicles-peoples@@

Over the centuries, they have developed their own ways of life, beliefs and answers to the question of what the state should actually be.

On Khar-Durim, a dwarf may first tell you which clan he comes from, and only then call himself an inhabitant of the island.

On Valoria, a man may serve a different lord than his neighbor, but both recognize the same crown.

On Sah'Rav, until recently, the answer was the simplest - above all stood the elven king.

Today there is no king anymore.

And perhaps that is why the three islands have never been so different from each other as they are now.

I. Khar-Durim - Four Clans

Dwarves have been saying for centuries that a mountain may have many peaks, but they all rise from the same earth.

For most of their history, however, this did not mean one kingdom.

Khar-Durim belonged to the Four Clans.

Each had its own leader, its own lands, traditions and responsibilities. They were united by culture, trade, faith and a common island, but no clan had the right to command the others.

This world ended when the armies of the Elven king Vaelthar arrived on Khar-Durim.

The four clans were defeated.

And for the next hundred years the dwarves lived under elven slavery.

Their mines worked for the elven empire. Their wealth was taken away from the island. Dwarven artisans crafted for foreign lords, and those who once defended their own lands found themselves disarmed, subjugated, and sometimes forced to police their own people.

Entire generations of dwarves were born and died without knowing the free Khar-Durim. Only recently have the four clans done something they couldn't do a hundred years earlier.

They stood together.

The uprising ended elven slavery and changed Khar-Durim forever.

Today, the Four Clans still exist.

For the first time, however, there is one king above them all.

Thorgrim Iron Crown.

This does not mean that all four view his crown in the same way.

Iron Hammers

If you ask a member of the Iron Hammers what a dwarf should do, you will probably hear two answers:

work and fight.

They had been miners and warriors of Khar-Duri for generations. Some of the island's wealth came from their mines, and their warriors fought to defend it.

The Elven occupation took one from them and exploited the other.

Miners still went underground, but extracted wealth for foreign masters. The former warriors were disarmed and some were forced to guard their own people.

The Iron Hammers have not forgotten this humiliation.

Of all the clans, this is the easiest place to find a dwarf who will spit at the word "elf".

It is also from the Iron Hammers that the man who ended his hundred-year captivity comes.

Thorgrim Iron Crown.

For his clan, he is above all a king who has done what no one else has been able to do for generations:

united Khar-Durim.

The headquarters of the Iron Hammers is Dur-Garim, a mountain city that is also the capital of the dwarven kingdom. Behind its monumental gate, carved into the mountainside, lie the royal halls and the treasury, a reminder of why Khar-Durim has aroused the interest of its neighbors for centuries.

The Iron Hammers regained their freedom.

They have not yet regained the ability to forget.

Stone Shields

Not everything that Khar-Durim protects must have an ax in its hand.

Stone Shields build things to last longer than their creators.

Walls.

Dear.

Gates.

Strongholds.

When other Clans are wondering how to win the next battle, Stoneshield will be more likely to ask how to make sure the next battle never reaches her home.

Their home, Kar-Dor, is more like a vast fortress than an ordinary dwarven city.

The Clan is committed to tradition and views the Copper Gears' inventions with some suspicion. This doesn't stop him from using their machines when the machine turns out to be better than the pickaxe.

Stone Shields do not like change for the sake of change.

Their current leader, Borgrim of the Stone Shields, is one of the few living dwarves who remembers Khar-Durim from before the Elven conquest.

He saw the fall of ancient fortifications.

He survived a hundred years of foreign rule.

And then he saw Thorgrim regain what his generation had lost.

Therefore, Borgrim's loyalty to the king is not based on admiration for the crown.

It comes from memory. For the Stone Shields, Thorgrim has proven that he can do one thing above all others:

keep the four clans together.

Copper Gears

In Brumwald, the hammer does not always strike the sword.

Sometimes it hits the gear.

The Copper Gears are the engineers, designers, and inventors of the Khar-Durim. They build mechanisms, improve the operation of mines, harness the power of water, and create machines that more traditional clans sometimes view with a mixture of suspicion and admiration.

Their Brumwald is also different from the other great dwarven settlements.

Around it there are fields, mills and granaries. It is here that much of Khar-Durim's food begins its journey towards the cities hidden among the mountains.

The Copper Gears believe that a nation's strength does not come solely from how heavy a hammer its warrior can lift.

Sometimes what's more important is whether someone can feed that warrior.

Or build a bridge for his army to cross.

Or a mechanism that will open the gate.

Today, the clan is ruled by young Eldrik.

His father, Haldrek, was one of the four leaders who helped Thorgrim liberate Khar-Durim.

Four went to Sah'Rava.

Three came back.

There are dwarves standing all over Khar-Durim today, ready to tell of Haldrek's heroism.

Eldrik had heard these stories enough times.

"They sent my father to a war he didn't want. Now they call him a hero so they don't have to call him dead."

The Copper Gears do not plan to rebel against Thorgrim.

They don't want another war. That's why they look with concern at those who, after one victory, began to wonder about the next one.

Deep Forges

In the far north of Khar-Durim stands a huge gate.

Behind it there is no road leading to the city.

Behind it is the city.

Gor-Dum was carved inside the mountain.

Houses, forges and great halls exist there in a world of stone, metal and fire. Lava flows through places where inhabitants of other lands would not even dare to live.

The Deep Forges have always been the most isolated of the four clans.

They are also the most religious.

For many of them, Groudon, the Father of the Earth and Mountains, is not just a character from an old legend.

It is the beginning of world order.

Their leader, Varkun of the Deep Forges, holds the title of Guardian of the First Fire.

It is in Gor-Dum that it is easiest to hear a view that the inhabitants of other clans often prefer not to express:

that Khar-Durim should not be satisfied with its regained freedom.

That if the dwarves could defeat the mightiest empire of Eryndor, perhaps they should use their strength.

That the world would be safer if ruled by those strong enough to defend it.

Thorgrim does not share these ambitions.

Varkun still recognizes Thorgrim as his king.

For now, these two things can be true at the same time.

Four clans are not four nations.

They are four answers to the question of what Khar-Durim should be. The Iron Hammers remember wrongdoing.

Stone Shields protect what has been recovered.

The Copper Gears look to what can be built.

The Deep Forges wonder how far their regained strength can reach.

Today there is one Iron Crown above them all.

How long?

Ask the four clans.

You will probably get four answers.

II. Valoria - The Human Kingdom

On Valoria, the question of affiliation is much simpler.

There are not four clans.

There are no four equal leaders.

There is a kingdom.

There is a crown on its top. Below her are the lords. Next, knights, merchants, craftsmen, farmers and inhabitants of cities and villages scattered around the island.

From Aldermar there are roads leading to fields, forests, ports and smaller settlements.

You'll often see the same motif above gates and shields:

Zamazenta.

The Great Protector.

For the people of Valoria, strength has long meant primarily the ability to protect what they already have.

Perhaps that is why the greatest war of recent generations never reached their lands.

Or perhaps the reason was much less romantic.

For most of recent events, Valoria has been ruled by Aldrin IV. His father left him a kingdom that was cautious, focused on its own affairs, and averse to conflict beyond its borders.

Aldrin was initially not much different from him.

Then the Elven King Vaelthar began to demand more and more.

Better trading conditions.

Access to ports.

Political concessions.

More privileges.

Aldrin looked at the conquered Khar-Durim and asked the question his father never had to ask:

what happens when the elves stop looking north and look towards Valoria?

He answered them in his typical way.

He didn't declare war.

He didn't send an army.

Officially, Valoria remained out of the conflict.

Unofficially, the situation was different.

The gun landed where it was supposed to go.

Food disappeared from warehouses and appeared in others.

Information crossed the sea.

Some ships saw more than their captains later remembered.

Aldrin helped the dwarves.

But he did it so that no Valorian soldier would have to march to the elven walls.

He was helped in this by a man whose name often appears at the royal court to this day:

Cedric Varen.

Cedric is not the hero of the song.

He probably wouldn't even want to become one. He is a man who believes that sometimes a few chests of gold, the right gossip, or the right message to the wrong man can achieve more than a thousand soldiers.

Lying is not a sin for him as long as he protects Valoria.

There is no shame in a bribe if it is cheaper than war.

And peace doesn't have to be friendship.

It is enough that it is better than the alternative.

Aldrin trusted him enough to entrust him with matters about which the official chronicles of the kingdom sometimes say very little.

Today, Cedric serves his daughter.

Elara II inherited her father's kingdom in a much more peaceful world.

She didn't inherit his character.

Where Aldrin was able to make a decision and accept its consequences, Elara is much more likely to wonder if there is a way to avoid the worst of them.

She is young.

Empathetic.

And much more interested in how the crown's decisions will affect ordinary people.

Her detractors might call this a weakness.

Her supporters - humanity.

Cedric would probably call it just another thing to consider.

However, they both agree on one thing:

Valoria doesn't need another war.

Elara because she doesn't want to see her people die.

Cedric because living subjects pay taxes much more regularly than dead ones.

Halflings also live on the sidelines of great politics.

Their small settlement is more interested in crops, weather, and what's on the table in the evening than in disputes between the crowns of Eryndor. Valoria leaves them alone.

Halflings are completely fine with this arrangement.

This may be one of the most successful political agreements in the entire archipelago.

Valoria has survived the last century without occupation.

Its cities were not burned.

Its fields did not become places of great battles.

Its kings did not go to elven prisons.

You could call it luck.

You could call it prudence.

You could also look at the actions of Aldrin and Cedric and conclude that Valoria simply learned very early that sometimes the best way to win a war is to never officially enter it.

III. Sah'Rava - Legacy of the Elves

If Khar-Durim is one kingdom today that remembers the times of division, Sah'Rava is its opposite.

Until recently it had one king.

One crown.

One army.

And one empire.

Today there are none of these things.

For centuries, elves have considered themselves a people particularly close to nature and its order.

Their Guardian was Xerneas, the Giver of Life.

From this belief, the idea of care was born.

From the idea of care - the belief that elves understand the world better than others. And from this it is only a step to say that since they know better, they should also decide for others.

More Sah'Rava peoples came under the elven crown.

Then her power crossed the sea.

For almost a hundred years, Khar-Durim also belonged to the empire.

The last elven king was Vaelthar.

When he died, he left no successor able to maintain what he had built.

But it was not the lack of a suitable king that ultimately divided the elves.

The problem was much deeper.

The three most powerful aristocratic families looked upon the ruins of the empire.

And everyone saw a different lesson in them.

Those who think Vaelthar was too weak

For the first house, defeat was not proof that Vaelthar had gone too far.

She was proof that he hadn't gone far enough.

He allowed the dwarves to keep their clans.

He allowed them to remember past leaders.

He allowed them to maintain their culture and the feeling that Khar-Durim still belonged to them.

And when the Uprising began, he deemed it unworthy of his own attention.

According to them, the idea of elven domination has not lost.

The elf who couldn't force her properly was the loser.

Among them, it is easiest to find those who still talk about the former empire with pride.

And those who believe that one day the elves should regain what they have lost.

Those who believe Vaelthar should never have set out

The other family looks at the same story and sees something completely different.

Before the invasion, Khar-Durim was a neighbor.

After that it became the enemy.

For a hundred years, the empire had to maintain garrisons, control mines, suppress resistance, and keep an eye on a people who never accepted elven rule.

And when these people finally rebelled, the four divided clans truly united for the first time.

The result?

Khar-Durim is free.

Vaelthar is dead.

The empire ceased to exist.

For this family, the conclusion is obvious:

the war should never have started.

This does not mean that they suddenly stopped considering elves as a special people.

It only means that they are not going to destroy their own home again trying to prove it to someone on the other side of the sea.

Those who believe that Vaelthar has chosen the wrong path

The third house still looks up to Xerneas more than the others.

He still talks about harmony.

About the natural order.

About the elves' responsibility for the world of which they are a part.

And that is why his views can be most deceptive to the newcomer.

They also condemn the captivity of Khar-Durim.

They condemn the occupation.

They condemn Vaelthar's violence.

But not necessarily because they consider dwarves to be equal to elves. In their opinion, Vaelthar confused leadership with dominion.

There was no need to capture the dwarven cities.

It was enough to control trade.

There was no need to put shackles on the dwarves.

It was possible to make their economy dependent.

There was no need to destroy the four clans.

They could be made to compete with each other and seek elven support.

According to them, elves should actually show others the right path.

They just need to do it smarter than Vaelthar.

For some, it is the most reasonable of the three families.

To others, just a softer-sounding version of the same hubris that created an empire.

And that is why after Vaelthar's death there was no new elven king.

Not because there were no elves wanting the crown.

Not because the dwarves forbade them from rebuilding the country.

The three houses couldn't even agree on why their world had fallen apart.

One said:

"Vaelthar was too weak."

Second:

"Vaelthar should never have invaded Khar-Durim."

Third:

"Vaelthar wanted to achieve the right goal in the worst possible way."

So everyone retreated to their own lands.

The crown was left without an owner.

And the elven kingdom ceased to exist. However, elves are not the only inhabitants of Sah'Rava.

They never were.

Nekhari

In the deserts of the east live the Nekhari.

Their bodies resemble the corpses of people who should have died generations ago.

However, they are not mindless dead.

They have their own cities, traditions and memories.

Long memory.

In their culture, the Passage is of particular importance, after which Nekhari's body stops aging like the body of an ordinary mortal.

This does not make them indestructible.

They can be killed.

Time simply stopped being the same enemy for them as it was for other peoples.

For years they were subject to the elven empire.

Today they decide about Nekhara again.

Zashara

The Zashara live in the western jungles.

A lizard people who, of all the inhabitants of Sah'Rava, are probably least concerned with who they believe to be the rightful ruler of the entire island.

Their communities are small.

Life is simple.

And territorial ambitions are practically non-existent.

They don't need an empire.

They don't need King Sah'Rava.

Above all, they want others to let them live their own lives. After the fall of Vaelthar, that's exactly what they did.

Goblins

Goblin tribes live on the savannas.

They did not create a great kingdom.

They have no common monarch.

Tribe, family and the memory of ancestors are much more important to them.

One of the most important places of their culture is the Ancestral House, dominated by Cubone's huge skull.

For years they had to pay tribute to the elven crown and send their men when the king demanded it.

When Vaelthar died, the goblins did not convene a council to debate Sah'Rava's future government.

They started celebrating.

And they stopped paying tribute.

Sah'Rava has no single nation today.

There is no one country.

There is not even a common answer to the question of whether the fall of the empire was a tragedy, a liberation or a wasted opportunity.

Perhaps he will never find her again.

Three islands

This is what Eryndor looks like when you arrive.

On Khar-Durim, four clans try to decide what to do with the freedom they have fought for for a hundred years.

On Valoria, the people want to maintain the peace their former king won without openly participating in war. On Sah'Rav, residents learn to live in a world where no one can anymore point to one crown and say:

“She rules the island.”

You don't have to take sides.

You don't even have to be interested in their disputes.

But if you're going to travel through Eryndor, it's good to know one thing:

where a man, dwarf or elf comes from will often tell you less about him than what he chooses to believe.

Perhaps after many days of traveling. Perhaps after a night where you were sure the sea wouldn't let you out again.

You won't be the first newcomer to set foot on these shores. You probably won't be the last either.

Before you lies Eryndor, an archipelago of three great islands and peoples whose histories have been intertwined long before your arrival.

To the north rises Khar-Durim. A land of mountains, deep mines and forges where dwarves have been working for generations. The riches hidden beneath its land have long aroused the envy of others, and over a hundred years ago they became one of the reasons why the island lost its freedom. For almost a century, Khar-Durim was under the rule of the elves.

Today, dwarven banners fly in the mountains again.

Captivity recently ended when four ancient clans stood together against the occupiers for the first time. Their leader was Thorgrim Ironcrown, the current king of Khar-Durim.

For some it is a liberator.

For others, a conqueror.

There are also those who use much worse terms.

On Valoria you will find a completely different world.

Vast fields are crossed by roads leading between villages and cities, and above them rise the castles of human lords. In the heart of the island lies Aldermar, the capital of the kingdom and the seat of the young Queen Elara II.

Valoria escaped the fate of Khar-Durim.

Elven armies never marched through her cities, and human armies never went openly to great war.

But that doesn't mean people were just looking at her.

The old King Aldrin IV left behind a kingdom that survived the greatest conflict of recent generations almost intact. Some will say that he achieved this through prudence. Others say it was through cunning. Still others will argue that one has never excluded the other.

Today Valoria wants one thing above all:

for the war to remain a thing of the past.

The southernmost point is Sah'Rava.

The jungles of the west give way to hot savannahs, and further east the land turns into desert.

Until recently, almost all of this belonged to the elven empire.

For generations, the elves subjugated the other peoples of Sah'Rava, and for almost a century their rule extended far beyond their own island - to the mines and cities of Khar-Durim.

Then their king died.

The empire has fallen.

Today, Sah'Rava has no single ruler.

Elves still inhabit the island, but they no longer rule the entire lands they once considered theirs. In the desert, the Nekhari decide for themselves again, whose bodies should have turned to dust a long time ago. In the jungles live the Zashara, a lizard people with little interest in the disputes of ancient kings. The goblin tribes regained their lands on the savannas.

Sah'Rava is the most divided part of Eryndor today.

And perhaps that is why no other island hides so many remnants of a world that not long ago seemed indestructible.

The war is over.

The armies returned home. Ships to ports. Battlefields are slowly becoming overgrown and the ruins are becoming part of the landscape.

Memory doesn't fade away that quickly.

The dwarves remember a hundred years of captivity.

The elves remember the lost empire. People remember the times when a few bad decisions were enough for war to reach their shores.

Nekhari remember orders they wish they had never followed.

Others are just glad that no one else is coming for their sons, gold, or land.

If you listen to the people of Eryndor long enough, you will soon discover something else.

Not everyone remembers the same story.

For a dwarven chronicler, one battle can be a great victory. The elf standing on the other side may give it a completely different name. What was considered reasonable neutrality to a Valorian may be called cowardice by another.

You can listen to them.

You can read the books they left behind.

You can visit the places they talk about.

And then you decide who to believe.

However, there are stories much older than the last war.

Older than Thorgrim.

Older than the elven kings.

Perhaps even older than the names Khar-Durim, Valorii, and Sah'Rava themselves.

The people of Eryndor have been talking about the Three Guardians for generations.

About Groudon, whom the dwarves call the Father of Earth and Mountains.

About Xerneas, whom the elves worship as the Giver of Life.

And about Zamazent, whom the people of Valoria see as the Great Protector.

Did they really create Eryndor?

Did they ever speak to its inhabitants?

Are the stories about them memories of real events, or just legends repeated so long that no one remembers how they began?

You will also get different answers to these questions. And now you appear on the shores of Eryndor.

There is no throne waiting for you.

There is no prophecy bearing your name.

No one expects you to end an ancient conflict or save the world.

Eryndor didn't need you to exist.

His kings loved and hated him. His armies won and lost. Cities rose, empires fell, and Pokémon lived alongside the inhabitants of these islands long before you saw their shores.

This is not the beginning of the history of Eryndor.

This is just the moment when you become its witness.

What you do next is up to you.

You can traverse the mountains of Khar-Durim, visit the cities of Valoria, or venture into the ruins of Sah'Rava. You can search for Pokémon, wealth, fame, knowledge, or just a place you haven't seen before.

And if you want to find out why this world looks like this...

Eryndor has many stories to tell.
